name: Fisher-Janis-Newman-Winicour Scalar Field
description: The static, spherically symmetric spacetime of a mass that also carries a massless scalar field, found by I. Z. Fisher in 1948 and found again by Allen Janis, Ezra Newman, and Jeffrey Winicour in 1968. For any scalar charge, however small, the sphere where Schwarzschild's horizon would stand has zero area and infinite curvature, and no horizon hides it.
convention: The parameter $b$ is a length and $\gamma$ a pure number, and the mass $M$ has $2GM/c^2 = \gamma b$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: What does gravity do to the scalar field of a point source? Iosif Zalmanovich Fisher asked it in 1947 of the meson field $Ge^{-\chi r}/r$ [fisher1948, malomuzh2009]. For a field with no mass, $\chi = 0$, he solved Einstein's equations exactly [fisher1948]. Close to the source the field grows only as a logarithm, the metric has no gravitational radius, and gravity, usually assumed negligible for elementary particles, changes the field completely [fisher1948]. The total energy of the static field still diverges, as a logarithm [fisher1948].¶With the areal radius as coordinate the metric can be written only implicitly, which is as far as Otto Bergmann and Roy Leipnik got when they found the solution again in 1957 [bergmann1957, bronnikov2011, abdolrahimi2010]. Every static vacuum metric has a reciprocal that is a vacuum solution too, with $g_{tt}$ inverted and the metric of space multiplied by $g_{tt}^2$, as Hans Buchdahl showed in 1954 [buchdahl1954]. His recipe of 1959 turns any static vacuum solution into a family of scalar field solutions "by inspection", and in spherical symmetry the recipe reaches every one of them [buchdahl1959reciprocal]. The names that stuck are those of Allen Janis, Ezra Newman, and Jeffrey Winicour, who called their paper of 1968 "Reality of the Schwarzschild Singularity" [janis1968, abdolrahimi2010]. In their words it is a solution "that coincides with the exterior ($r>2m$) Schwarzschild solution, but where the Schwarzschild 'sphere' becomes a point singularity" [janis1968]. To Max Wyman, who returned to Bergmann and Leipnik's problem in 1981, "the integration of the field equations is almost trivial" in another coordinate system [wyman1981].¶Whose solution is it? The form used today, $g_{tt} = -(1 - b/r)^{\gamma}$, is A. G. Agnese and M. La Camera's rewriting of Wyman's solution in 1985 [agnese1985, virbhadra1997]. K. S. Virbhadra settled half of it in 1997: with $r = R + r_0(\mu + 1)/2$ Wyman's solution is Janis, Newman, and Winicour's, so "Wyman did not obtain a new solution" [virbhadra1997]. For English readers there is K. G. Zloshchastiev's translation of Fisher's paper, made in 1999 "to clarify the historically important question who was the pioneer" [fisher1948]. By his account Janis, Newman, and Winicour had "rediscovered (in other coordinates)" a solution twenty years old [fisher1948]. Fisher wrote his metric in the areal radius through a function $Z(r)$, and $Z/c$ is the radius $R$ that Janis, Newman, and Winicour took for their coordinate [fisher1948, virbhadra1997].¶A scalar field, however weak, removes Schwarzschild's horizon [virbhadra1997, abdolrahimi2010]. For every $\gamma < 1$ the sphere $r = b$ has zero area and infinite curvature, with nothing to hide it [virbhadra1997, abdolrahimi2010]. Agnese and La Camera made a slogan of it, "Gravitation without black holes": add a massless scalar field, and the event horizons of the Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordström, and Kerr solutions "all reduce to a point" [agnese1985]. The general statement is J. E. Chase's theorem of 1970: every massless scalar field that is gravitationally coupled, static, and asymptotically flat "becomes singular at a simply-connected event horizon" [chase1970]. In Jacob Bekenstein's proof of 1972 a static black hole "cannot have any exterior classical scalar or massive vector fields" [bekenstein1972].¶The solution is at its simplest in the harmonic coordinate $u$ that Kirill Bronnikov used in 1973, where the scalar field is a constant times $u$ and the metric is built from $e^{-2mu}$ and $\sinh(ku)$ [bronnikov1973, bronnikov2011]. Change the sign of the field's energy and $\sinh$ becomes $\sin$: the singularity opens into the throat of the wormhole that Homer Ellis published the same year, a member of the family now called anti-Fisher by analogy with de Sitter and anti-de Sitter [bronnikov2011, ellis1973]. The static solution is also unstable: in Bronnikov and A. V. Khodunov's analysis of 1979, spherically symmetric perturbations of it grow exponentially [bronnikov1979, bronnikov2011]. Under Fisher's name, Shohreh Abdolrahimi and Andrey Shoom studied the solution in 2010 in any number of dimensions, where Basilis Xanthopoulos and Thomas Zannias had integrated it in isotropic coordinates in 1989 [abdolrahimi2010, xanthopoulos1989]. They drew its Penrose diagram, with the singularity a timelike line, and embedded its equatorial plane: in ordinary flat space outside the sphere where the Misner-Sharp energy vanishes, and in a flat space with one timelike direction inside it, where that energy is negative [abdolrahimi2010]. The singularity divides the manifold in two, and they named the part on its far side the Fisher universe, an anisotropic cosmology that expands and contracts between a "Big Bang" and a "Big Crunch" [abdolrahimi2010].¶What would such an object look like? A scalar charge changes the bending of light, and K. S. Virbhadra, D. Narasimha, and S. M. Chitre worked out by how much in 1998 [virbhadra1998]. The photon sphere is $r = b(1 + 2\gamma)/2$, and it exists only for $\gamma > 1/2$ [claudel2001]. A singularity inside at least one photon sphere is "weakly naked" and one inside none is "strongly naked", in Virbhadra and George Ellis's sorting of 2002 [virbhadra2002]. A weakly naked singularity lenses much as Schwarzschild's black hole does, and a strongly naked one makes either two Einstein rings or none and no relativistic images [virbhadra2002]. The Event Horizon Telescope collaboration, testing the solution on its image of Sagittarius A* in 2022, concluded that the possibility that the object is a naked singularity "cannot be ruled out based on the metric tests" it had performed [eht2022metric].

related.text: The case with no scalar field, $\gamma = 1$, where $r = b$ is the horizon $r_s$. Add the smallest scalar charge and that sphere shrinks to a point of infinite curvature [janis1968].

The same $g_{tt} = -(1 - b/r)^{\gamma}$ with no scalar field: Zipoy and Voorhees's metric stays a vacuum and loses its spherical symmetry. Anirban Chowdhury, Mandar Patil, Daniele Malafarina, and Pankaj Joshi worked out the accretion disks of both side by side in 2012 [chowdhury2012].

Flip the sign of the scalar field's energy and Fisher's solution becomes the anti-Fisher family, whose member with no mass is this wormhole. In the harmonic coordinate the change is $\sinh(ku) \to \sin(ku)$ [bronnikov1973, bronnikov2011].
The same massless scalar field falling in from infinity. Fisher's singularity is there from the start, and Roberts found his solution while looking for one that develops [roberts1996].
A scalar field that holds together with no singularity. Give the field a mass and let its phase turn at a frequency $\omega$, and gravity binds it into a star with a regular centre [liebling2023].

The limit $\gamma \to \infty$ with $\gamma b = 2m$ held fixed, where $f^\gamma \to e^{-2m/r}$. It takes the scalar field's energy negative, and the naked singularity opens into the throat of a wormhole [makukov2018].
The homogeneous solution of the same field equations, Einstein's with a massless scalar field, with a different rate of expansion along each axis [belinskii1973].

Fisher's metric divided by a scalar field. In Brans's constants $C$ and $\lambda$, with $\phi/\phi_0 = f^{C/2\lambda}$ and $\gamma = (C + 2)/2\lambda$, the metric $g_{\mu\nu}\phi_0/\phi$ solves the vacuum equations of Brans and Dicke's theory, where freely falling bodies follow its geodesics [dicke1962, faraoni2018].

coordinates.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Value of $r$ at the singularity, a length: $b = 2\sqrt{G^2M^2/c^4 + q^2}$ for a mass $M$ and a scalar charge $q$, itself a length

Share of the mass in $b$, a pure number with $0 < \gamma \le 1$: $\gamma = 2GM/(c^2b)$; $\gamma = 1$ is Schwarzschild's metric with $r_s = b$. A radial light ray keeps $ct \mp r_*$ for the tortoise coordinate $r_*$, with $dr_*/dr = (1 - b/r)^{-\gamma}$
Schwarzschild's function with $b$ for $r_s$; the scalar field is $\varphi = \sqrt{(1 - \gamma^2)c^4/16\pi G}\,\ln f$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ that are Schwarzschild's at $\gamma = 1$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length, and write $f = 1 - b/r$. The areal radius is $rf^{(1-\gamma)/2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Janis-Newman-Winicour

parameters.description: A length: $b = 2\sqrt{G^2M^2/c^4 + q^2}$ for a mass $M$ and a scalar charge $q$, itself a length

Share of the mass in $b$, a pure number with $0 < \gamma \le 1$: $\gamma = 2GM/(c^2b)$; $\gamma = 1$ is Schwarzschild's metric with $r_s = b$. A radial light ray keeps $ct \mp r_*$ for the tortoise coordinate $r_*$, with $dr_*/dr = (1 - b/r)^{-\gamma}$
The ratio $1 - b/r$ of the spherical chart; the scalar field is $\varphi = \sqrt{(1 - \gamma^2)c^4/16\pi G}\,\ln f$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, R, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $R = r - b(1 + \gamma)/2$ a length, and write $f = (2R - b(1 - \gamma))/(2R + b(1 + \gamma))$. Janis, Newman, and Winicour's parameters are $r_0 = \gamma b$ and $\mu = 1/\gamma$, and Fisher's function is $Z = cR$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{R} + \dfrac{2b\,\gamma\,f^{2\gamma}}{\left(2R + b\left(1 + \gamma\right)\right)\left(2R - b\left(1 - \gamma\right)\right)}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{2b\,\gamma}{\left(2R + b\left(1 + \gamma\right)\right)\left(2R - b\left(1 - \gamma\right)\right)}\dot{R}^2 - R\,\dot{\theta}^2 - R\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Isotropic

parameters.description: Four times the value of $\rho$ at the singularity, a length: $b = 2\sqrt{G^2M^2/c^4 + q^2}$ for a mass $M$ and a scalar charge $q$, itself a length

Share of the mass in $b$, a pure number with $0 < \gamma \le 1$: $\gamma = 2GM/(c^2b)$; $\gamma = 1$ is Schwarzschild's metric with $r_s = b$. A radial light ray keeps $ct \mp r_*$ for the tortoise coordinate $r_*$, with $dr_*/dr = (1 - b/r)^{-\gamma}$

The square root of the ratio $1 - b/r$ of the spherical chart; the scalar field is $\varphi = \sqrt{(1 - \gamma^2)c^4/4\pi G}\,\ln h$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ the isotropic radius, a length with $r = \rho\left(1 + b/4\rho\right)^2$, and write $h = (4\rho - b)/(4\rho + b)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{\rho} + \dfrac{2048b\,\gamma\,\rho^4\,h^{4\gamma}}{\left(4\rho - b\right)^3\left(4\rho + b\right)^3}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{2b\left(4\gamma\,\rho - b\right)}{\rho\left(4\rho - b\right)\left(4\rho + b\right)}\dot{\rho}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(16\rho^2 - 8b\,\gamma\,\rho + b^2\right)}{\left(4\rho - b\right)\left(4\rho + b\right)}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(16\rho^2 - 8b\,\gamma\,\rho + b^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{\left(4\rho - b\right)\left(4\rho + b\right)}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Harmonic

parameters.description: Mass as a length, $m = GM/c^2 = \gamma b/2$, with $0 < m \le k$; $m = k$ is Schwarzschild's metric

A length, $k = b/2 = \sqrt{m^2 + q^2}$ for a scalar charge $q$; the scalar field is $\varphi = -\sqrt{(k^2 - m^2)c^4/4\pi G}\,u$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, u, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $u$ an inverse length, the harmonic coordinate with $e^{-2ku} = 1 - b/r$. The lengths are $k = b/2$ and $m = \gamma b/2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
